title: Spanish foundations
description: Four A1 Spanish lessons: first words, introductions, polite café requests, and numbers for everyday quantities. Native-speaker editorial review remains open.

units.title: Getting around
units.objective: Understand prices and quantities in everyday errands.

units.title: Finding your way
units.objective: Ask where things are and follow spoken directions.

units.title: Everyday life
units.objective: Talk about days, times, and the people around you.

concepts.title: First words and greetings
concepts.explanation: Spanish greets by the hour, and it greets in the plural even for a single morning: buenos días, buenas tardes. The habit worth starting on day one is that Spanish marks a question twice, with an upside-down question mark at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so you can see a question coming before you have read a word of it.
concepts.commonError: Say hola the moment you arrive. Save adiós for leaving.

concepts.title: Introducing yourself
concepts.explanation: Spanish says Me llamo Ana, literally 'I call myself Ana'; the verb llamarse carries a pronoun that points back at the speaker. Asking the same question of someone else changes that pronoun to te: ¿Cómo te llamas? Soy Ana is the plain alternative, built on 'to be'.
concepts.commonError: Use me llamo for your own name and te llamas in the informal question. Do not swap me and te.

concepts.title: Polite café requests
concepts.explanation: For a polite café request Spanish uses quisiera, 'I would like', instead of the blunter quiero: Quisiera un café, por favor. The article stays un for either drink, and café and té keep their accents.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.

concepts.commonError: Keep un with café and té in these requests. Remember the accents in café and té.

concepts.title: Numbers and quantities
concepts.explanation: Spanish runs one to ten as ordinary digits, then glues the parts of a number together where English keeps them apart: dieciséis for sixteen, veintiuno for twenty-one. That gluing stops at thirty, where a separate y appears, treinta y uno. A number in front of a noun also has to agree with it: un café is one coffee, but una manzana is one apple.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Use cuánto for the price of one item. Keep una with manzana because it is feminine.

concepts.title: Asking the way
concepts.explanation: Spanish marks the asking word with a written accent: dónde asks 'where', while the same letters without it, donde, are not asking anything. The accent does not change how the word sounds; it tells you what the word is doing, and a direct question also opens with ¿ and closes with ?. Ask about a place with estar, ¿Dónde está la estación?, and learn the directions as chunks: todo recto, a la izquierda, a la derecha, with luego joining the second step to the first.

examples.target: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

concepts.commonError: Dónde asks where. Quién asks who and qué asks what. The accent on dónde marks the question and drops in the middle of a sentence.

concepts.title: Prices and paying
concepts.explanation: A Spanish question wears two marks, an upside-down one at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so ¿Cuánto cuesta? announces itself before you read a word. Costar changes its stem under stress: cuesta for a single item, cuestan for several, and never costa. The bill is la cuenta, a feminine noun, and por favor is the politeness that travels with it.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

concepts.commonError: Spanish puts no before the verb, never after it. Cost is cuesta for one thing and cuestan for several.

concepts.title: Days and times
concepts.explanation: Five Spanish weekdays are the old sky names — lunes (moon), martes (Mars), miércoles (Mercury), jueves (Jupiter), viernes (Venus) — while sábado and domingo come from the Sabbath and the Lord’s day. They are masculine and lower-case, and the article el carries the meaning of ‘on’: el lunes. Mañana is tomorrow; la mañana is the morning.
concepts.commonError: Mañana is both tomorrow and morning. La mañana is the morning; mañana alone in a schedule usually means tomorrow.

concepts.title: Family and people
concepts.explanation: Spanish shows a noun's gender in its article — el hermano, la hermana — and hides an irregular verb under the simplest sentence: yo tengo, never yo tene. The possessive mi does not change with who is speaking; it changes with how many people are being counted, so mi hermana is one sister and mis hermanas is two, whoever the speaker is.
concepts.commonError: Tengo, not tene. Tener is irregular in the I form and it is the form you use most when talking about family.

vocabulary.example: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.

lessons.title: First words
lessons.objective: Greet someone in Spanish, and meet the opening question mark that Spanish puts in front.
lessons.explanation: Spanish greets by the hour, and it greets in the plural even for a single morning: buenos días, buenas tardes. The habit worth starting on day one is that Spanish marks a question twice, with an upside-down question mark at the front and an ordinary one at the end, so you can see a question coming before you have read a word of it.
lessons.culturalNote: Hola works everywhere, all day. Gracias answers everything from gifts to directions.

exercises.prompt: A friend says this to you in Madrid before anything else is said. What does «Hola» mean?
exercises.explanation: Hola needs no clock. Morning, afternoon or night, this is the greeting that works.

exercises.prompt: Spanish opens a question with an upside-down mark and closes it with an ordinary one. Which of these is asking something?
exercises.explanation: Only the first line is a question: it carries the upside-down opening mark and the closing one. The other two are statements and need neither.

exercises.prompt: You meet a friend in Madrid. Greet them before anything else is said.
exercises.explanation: One word is all this needs. Say it aloud before you check.

exercises.prompt: Complete the greeting you give a friend: ___
exercises.explanation: Hola comes first; the rest of the sentence waits.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange and count the questions in it.
exercises.explanation: Two of the lines open with the upside-down mark. The other four are statements.

exercises.prompt: Write down both words. The second one is a thank you.
exercises.explanation: Hola first, then gracias.

lessons.title: Introducing yourself
lessons.objective: Introduce yourself with the reflexive verb llamarse and ask a name with the pronoun that travels with it.
lessons.explanation: Spanish does not say 'my name is'. It says Me llamo Ana, literally 'I call myself Ana' — the small me is part of the verb llamarse and points back at the speaker. Turn the same verb on the person in front of you and that me becomes te: ¿Cómo te llamas? Soy Ana is the other introduction, and that one uses plain 'to be'. The pronoun, not the verb, is what changes.
lessons.culturalNote: The name question uses informal te for a peer. In a more formal situation, Spanish also has an usted form; this lesson stays with the informal question.

exercises.prompt: Me llamo Ana and Soy Ana both give a name. Which one uses the verb that literally means 'I call myself'?
exercises.explanation: Me llamo Ana is the reflexive form — 'I call myself Ana'. Soy Ana uses ser ('to be'), and ¿Cómo te llamas? is the question.

exercises.prompt: Ask a classmate their name with the question whose pronoun changes to te.
exercises.explanation: The verb is the same one as in Me llamo, but the pronoun turns into te when it points at the person you are speaking to.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange. Which short word tells you the first speaker is talking about herself?
exercises.explanation: Me is the reflexive pronoun: it turns the verb llamarse back on the person speaking. The other introduction uses soy instead.
exercises.passage:
— ¡Hola! Me llamo Ana.
— Mucho gusto, Ana. Soy Leo.
— Encantada, Leo.
exercises.translation:
— Hello! My name is Ana.
— Nice to meet you, Ana. I am Leo.
— Nice to meet you, Leo.

exercises.prompt: A neighbour introduces herself to you. Give the two-word Spanish reply that closes an introduction.
exercises.explanation: Mucho gusto closes an introduction, and the sentence needs no pronoun.

exercises.prompt: The words are jumbled. Build the reflexive sentence that gives Ana's name.
exercises.explanation: Me llamo Ana puts the reflexive pronoun first, then the verb, then the name.

exercises.prompt: A classmate has introduced herself. Introduce yourself the same way, as Ana, using the verb that needs a pronoun.
exercises.explanation: Say the whole reflexive phrase; leaving out me would leave the verb belonging to nobody.

lessons.title: At the café
lessons.objective: Ask for a drink with the softened verb quisiera, and keep the accents on café and té.
lessons.explanation: Quiero means 'I want', and in a café it can sound blunt. Spanish softens the same verb into quisiera, 'I would like', and that ending is the whole difference: Quisiera un café, por favor. The article un does not change with the drink — Quisiera un té, por favor — so only the noun moves. Keep the accents: café and té each carry one, and por favor is the phrase that turns the request into a courteous one.

examples.meaning: I would like a coffee, please.
I would like a tea, please.

lessons.culturalNote: A greeting before a request and thanks afterward make this small exchange courteous.

exercises.prompt: Quiero and quisiera are the same verb. Which request is the softened, polite one?
exercises.explanation: Quisiera gives the verb a conditional ending, and that is what makes the request courteous. Quiero is the blunt form.

exercises.prompt: Ask for tea politely, using the softened verb rather than quiero.
exercises.explanation: Same polite frame, tea instead of coffee: Quisiera un té, por favor, with the accent on té.

exercises.prompt: Read the café exchange. How many drinks does the customer order?
exercises.explanation: The customer asks for a té and then adds un café, so two drinks in all.
exercises.passage:
— ¡Buenas! Quisiera un té, por favor.
— ¿Un té?
— Sí, y un café también. Gracias.
exercises.translation:
— Hello! I would like a tea, please.
— A tea?
— Yes, and a coffee too. Thank you.

exercises.prompt: What does this café line mean in English: Quisiera un café, por favor.
answers: I would like a coffee, please.
exercises.explanation: Quisiera is 'I would like', and por favor supplies the 'please'.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to build the polite request for one coffee.
exercises.explanation: Quisiera opens it, the drink follows with un, and por favor finishes the request.

exercises.prompt: You reach the counter and want a coffee. Make the short polite request, without the verb.
exercises.explanation: Un café, por favor — the short request drops quisiera but keeps por favor.

lessons.title: Numbers and quantities
lessons.objective: Count one to ten, then see how Spanish welds a whole number such as veintiuno into a single written word.
lessons.explanation: Spanish counts one to ten straight. The stretch that surprises English speakers is the twenties: veintiuno, veintidós, veintitrés, written as one word, the same way dieciséis and diecisiete glue their parts together. The separate y arrives only at thirty-one, treinta y uno. Because the number agrees with its noun, one is un with a masculine café and una with a feminine manzana.

examples.meaning: How much does a coffee cost?

lessons.culturalNote: Prices may be said quickly. First listen for the number, then the item and the total.

exercises.prompt: Three is hiding inside veintitrés, glued to veinte. Which Spanish word is it?
exercises.explanation: Tres is three. The twenties simply glue a number onto veinte, so veintitrés is twenty-three.

exercises.prompt: Read the price board. How much is the tea?
exercises.passage:
Café: dos euros.
Té: tres euros.
exercises.translation:
Coffee: two euros.
Tea: three euros.
exercises.explanation: The board prices tea at tres euros. Dos and tres behave here exactly as they did when you counted.

exercises.prompt: Put the Spanish words in order to ask the price of one coffee.
exercises.explanation: ¿Cuánto cuesta? is the price question as a unit, and the upside-down question mark opens the sentence. Un café follows it.

exercises.prompt: Say in Spanish: Two apples, please.
exercises.explanation: Manzanas is feminine plural, so 'one' would be una, but two is dos either way, only the word for one changes with the noun.

exercises.prompt: Think: a fruit seller has one apple but no sign. Ask the price in Spanish, then write the question.
exercises.explanation: One apple is una manzana, with the feminine una. The price question itself never changes.

lessons.title: Asking the way
lessons.objective: Learn the accent that turns donde into a question, then trace a set of directions step by step.
lessons.explanation: Spanish writes a question with an opening ¿ and a closing ?, and it puts an accent on donde only when the word is asking: ¿Dónde está la estación? is a question, while donde on its own is not. Places are asked about with estar, and the directions come as ready-made chunks, todo recto and a la izquierda, with luego joining the second step to the first. Perdone literally means 'forgive me' and turns the bare question polite.

examples.target: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
examples.meaning: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

lessons.culturalNote: In Spain you open a request to a stranger with Perdone, and you thank them even for one sentence of directions.

exercises.prompt: Three of these give a direction; the fourth is asking. Which single word is the asking one?
exercises.explanation: Dónde means where, and the written accent is there because the word is asking. Quién does the same job for a person, qué for a thing.

exercises.prompt: Put the Spanish words in order to ask where the station is.
exercises.explanation: The question opens with ¿ and its asking word dónde, and estar supplies está. Estación is feminine, so its article is la.

exercises.prompt: Ask in Spanish where the bathroom is. Baño is masculine.
exercises.explanation: Only the noun and its article change inside ¿Dónde está?; el marks the masculine baño. The accent on dónde stays, because the word is still asking.

exercises.prompt: Complete the directions: Todo recto, luego a la ___
exercises.explanation: Izquierda is left. Derecha is the opposite, and a la is fixed in front of both of them.

exercises.prompt: Soften the question by putting Perdone in front: ¿Dónde está la estación?
exercises.explanation: Perdone goes ahead of the question and a comma separates it. The accent on dónde stays, because it is still the word asking where.

exercises.prompt: Read the exchange and find the first direction the visitor is given.
exercises.explanation: The first instruction is todo recto, straight ahead. The second follows luego: a la izquierda.
exercises.passage:
Turista: Perdone, ¿dónde está el baño?
Señora: Todo recto, luego a la izquierda.
Turista: ¡Muchas gracias!
exercises.translation:
Tourist: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?
Woman: Straight ahead, then to the left.
Tourist: Many thanks!

lessons.title: Prices and paying
lessons.objective: Ask a price inside Spanish's two question marks, and make costar agree with one thing or with several.
lessons.explanation: A Spanish question wears two marks, the first one upside down, so ¿Cuánto cuesta? shows itself to be a question before you read a word of it. Costar changes its stem under stress — cuesta for a single item and cuestan for several, never costa. The bill is la cuenta, and por favor is what turns a statement into a polite request.

examples.meaning: How much does the coffee cost?

lessons.culturalNote: In many Spanish bars the bill comes when you ask for it, so la cuenta, por favor is the normal way to end a meal.

exercises.prompt: Spanish fences a question with two marks, the first of them upside down. Which of these is asking the price?
exercises.explanation: ¿Cuánto cuesta? is the price question: cuánto asks how much, cuesta comes from costar, and both marks are obligatory.

exercises.prompt: The stall is charging more than you expected. Put the words in order to say this is very expensive.
exercises.explanation: Muy sits immediately before caro, and esto is the 'this' that stands alone without a noun after it.

exercises.prompt: There is just one coffee, so costar keeps its singular form. Fill the blank: ¿___ cuesta el café?
exercises.explanation: Cuánto cuesta is the fixed frame, and the upside-down mark is already printed in front for you.

exercises.prompt: At a café in Seville you are pricing one coffee only. Ask the question.
exercises.explanation: Cuesta is singular because one coffee is being priced; for several the verb would turn into cuestan.

exercises.prompt: You think the price is fair. Turn «Es caro.» into its opposite.
exercises.explanation: No goes before the verb es; Spanish never lets the negation wander to the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Dinner in Madrid is over and you want to settle up. Ask the waiter for the bill.
exercises.explanation: Cuenta is feminine, so it takes la, and por favor is what keeps the request polite.

lessons.title: Days and times
lessons.objective: Five Spanish weekdays are the old planets and gods; learn which two days break that pattern.
lessons.explanation: Spanish weekdays are the Roman sky turned into a calendar: lunes is the moon, martes Mars, miércoles Mercury, jueves Jupiter and viernes Venus. Then the naming breaks — sábado comes from the Sabbath and domingo from the Lord’s day. The days are masculine and lower-case, and Spanish needs no separate word for ‘on’: the article el carries it, as in el lunes. Watch out, too: mañana is tomorrow, while la mañana is the morning.
lessons.culturalNote: Spanish weekdays are not capitalised, which is why lunes looks the same mid-sentence as at the start of one.

exercises.prompt: Your Madrid phone writes a label above the date. Tap the label for today.
exercises.explanation: That is hoy. The decoys mean tomorrow, Monday and the week.

exercises.prompt: Build the Spanish sentence for on Monday I work; the article carries the on.
exercises.explanation: El sits in front of the day and means on: el lunes, on Monday.

exercises.prompt: Complete the Spanish for on Mondays, meaning every Monday: ___ lunes trabajo.
exercises.explanation: Spanish uses the plural article for a repeated day: los lunes, on Mondays.

exercises.prompt: Predict the sentence before you write it: today is Friday.
exercises.explanation: Hoy es plus the day. Viernes still carries the name of Venus.

exercises.prompt: Give the English meaning: El lunes trabajo.
exercises.explanation: There is no separate word for on here; the article el does that work in front of the day.

exercises.prompt: Five Spanish weekdays carry the name of a planet or a god. Which pair leaves that company?
exercises.explanation: Sábado comes from the Sabbath and domingo from the Lord's day; lunes to viernes are the old sky names.

exercises.prompt: Read the week. Which day does the passage name after the moon?
exercises.passage: El lunes es el día de la Luna. El martes trabajo. El miércoles estudio. El jueves llamo a mi madre. El viernes descanso.
exercises.translation: Monday is the day of the moon. On Tuesday I work. On Wednesday I study. On Thursday I call my mother. On Friday I rest.
exercises.explanation: The first line says it: el lunes is the day of la Luna, the moon.

lessons.title: Family and people
lessons.objective: Say how many brothers and sisters you have, and let mi or mis follow the number you name.
lessons.explanation: Spanish shows a noun's gender in its article — el hermano, la hermana — and hides an irregular verb under the simplest sentence, since the I form of tener is tengo and never tene. The possessive mi does not change with who is speaking; it changes with how many are counted, so mi hermana is one sister and mis hermanas is two.
lessons.culturalNote: Familia in Spanish often stretches to grandparents, aunts and cousins, not just the household.

exercises.prompt: One letter separates the Spanish words for brother and sister. Which of these four is the sister?
exercises.explanation: Hermana is the sister; the -a ending marks her feminine, as -o marks hermano. Padres is the pair of parents, and la familia is the household.

exercises.prompt: Parents is plural, and so is the possessive in front of it. Fill the gap: Mis ___ viven en Madrid.
exercises.explanation: Padres is plural, which is why the verb is viven rather than vive.

exercises.prompt: Hermana is feminine and keeps the same article as the subject. Choose the line that correctly says I have a sister.
exercises.explanation: Una hermana keeps the feminine article una; un hermana and unos hermana are the two ways learners get this wrong.

exercises.prompt: You are describing the one brother you have. Predict the form before you write it: I have a brother.
exercises.explanation: Tener is irregular, so the I form is tengo and never tene: Tengo un hermano.

exercises.prompt: Turn the scattered words into a sentence that presents your family.
exercises.explanation: Familia is feminine, so the demonstrative is esta and the possessive is mi: Esta es mi familia.

exercises.prompt: Read what Ana wrote about her family. Which city are the parents still in?
exercises.explanation: The brother and sister are in Seville and Valencia; the closing sentence keeps the parents in Madrid.
exercises.passage: Mi familia no es muy grande. Mi hermano mayor se llama Max y trabaja en Sevilla; mi hermana Ana estudia en Valencia. Mis padres siguen viviendo en Madrid.
exercises.translation: My family is not very big. My older brother is called Max and works in Seville; my sister Ana studies in Valencia. My parents still live in Madrid.

exercises.prompt: Make the sentence talk about two sisters instead of one: Tengo una hermana.
exercises.explanation: The plural adds -s to hermana, and una becomes dos: Tengo dos hermanas.
